title: Does the aesthetic through line that connects Ghost World, Napoleon Dynamite and Dinner in America have a name?

commenti.body: I haven't seen Dinner in America, but it sounds to me like you could be describing an aesthetic of alienation, one characterized in part by anachronisms. The people in Napoleon Dynamite and Ghost World have fringe tastes that come out of their personalities, clothing, music preference, and decor. They're attracted to the out of place and time, and that alienates them from the world at large.

I haven’t seen Dinner in America, but Ghost World and Napoleon Dynamite are both heavily draped in irony, and I suspect that’s at least partly what you’re referring to. Both films would be very difficult for someone outside their cultural framework to understand, since the filmmakers’ intentions are so often opposite from the surface or superficial meanings of things.

The use of nostalgia you mention is a good example, where things that superficially appear pleasantly old-timey and simple are actually deconstructed, things superficially framed as beautiful are meant to be understood as ugly, and so on. To a member of the target audience, these are obvious, but if you miss out on the irony, the films are difficult to comprehend.

I remember someone at Netflix, back in theDVD-by-mail days, saying Napoleon Dynamite was one of the most difficult films for their algorithm to recommend, because its heavily ironic nature made it impossible to tell who would like it.

If you had to refer to this aesthetic what would you call it? What's the history of it? It's so iconic Im kind of amazed I dont know anything about it. It has so many different ingredients it's hard to pin down, similar to trying to pin down or distill the Wes Anderson aesthetic.

Oh, PS; watch Dinner In America. It's the funniest and weirdest movie Ive seen in a llooong time.
Burbcore

I know what you mean. I can't think of a term that some established writer probably has given it, but it's just described as a turn-of-the-century era 'quirky' class of films. There's a dry, indie low-budget look to it. Coming out of post-modernist aesthetics established in 90s. Awkward characters, quirky interests and behaviors from outsiders/wallflowers, pops of primary colors amid drabby, peachy/beige/white ones. I think it's more specifically at the tail-end of postmodernist era where they're getting more sardonic and ironic with it. the 'Losers' era of the 'Slacker' era.

I'd put my vote in for "Clowes-ian" after Dan Clowes. He's the cartoonist who wrote Ghost World and has done plenty of concept work for Wes Anderson. If you dig the style in these films, definitely check out his work and start with Eightball, his one-man anthology from the 90s and where Ghost World was originally serialized.

Yes, its very culturally coded.

But believe it or not, “Nacho Libre” achieved the same aesthetic but in rural mexico. As s Mexican-american, who grew up in both countries, I can appreciate both.

But it’s something I have never heard non-Mexicans mention. Presumably the subtle references go over their head, because its an alien culture to them.

Not surprisingly, Nacho Libre and Napoleon Dynamite share a director.
Hadnt heard of him but ill look him up.

The three films you mention do have many commonalities, but might I suggest that they are united by a tone.  I'd call this tone *deadpan.*

I'd say that **American Splendor** (2003) has a similar vibe.

Nicolaas Mink thinks Napoleon Dynamite is a western:

https://www.jstor.org/stable/25443688?mag=napoleon-dynamite-neo-western-film

>yet deeply hopeless

Napoleon Dynamite isn't hopeless (or ironic), at all. It is very sincere.

With Napoleon's help:

- Pedro organizes a willing coalition of social outcasts who challenge the implicit white supremacy in Preston, ID.

- Kip finds the courage to leave Idaho to be with a beautiful woman who sees his value.

- Uncle Rico realizes that reconciling with his romantic partner is more important that trying to return to a past that had no use for him.

With Deb's help, Napoleon finds someone to play tetherball with.

I would say that Napoloeon Dynamite is a riposte to Wes Anderson's work (which is draped in hopeful irony).

I would pair it with Taika Waititi's early work like Boy and Eagle vs Shark (my god, Eagle vs Shark owes so much to it).
